# Learning more about Coefficient Giving

## Our mission 

Our mission is “to do as much good as we can with the resources that are available to us.” 

  

This might seem broad and vague — it is deliberately so\! While many foundations and non-profits choose their causes first, Coefficient Giving works differently: we use rigorous analysis and evidence to guide us to the most promising opportunities to help others. We look for areas that are important (affect many lives), neglected (receive less attention than their importance warrants), and tractable (could be meaningfully progressed with additional resources).  This approach has led us to work across seemingly disparate funds, from [Global Health & Wellbeing Opportunities](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/global-health-wellbeing-opportunities/) to [Navigating Transformative AI](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/navigating-transformative-ai/). In the future, we might add, subtract, or change funds depending on where we think we can have the most impact.

  

## Recommended resources 

While reviewing these resources is optional, we've gathered them to give candidates a deeper understanding of our work, history, and organizational culture. We welcome feedback on this material — feel free to reach out to [jobs@coefficientgiving.org](mailto:jobs@openphilanthropy.org) with any questions or thoughts\!

  

### **Higher-priority resources**

  - Our cause prioritization team tackles the question of how to allocate our resources across different causes for maximum impact. [This page](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/strategic-cause-selection/) provides more information on our three strategic cause selection criteria: importance, neglectedness, and tractability. 
  - Our [Operating Values](https://coefficientgiving.org/our-approach/operating-values/) are the foundation of our culture. Far from being theoretical or purely aspirational, our team frequently and concretely references these values in our day-to-day work. 
  - [This blog post](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/open-philanthropy-is-now-coefficient-giving/), written by our CEO Alexander Berger, explains our rebrand to Coefficient Giving and our strategy to make philanthropy more efficient by helping more donors fund high-impact opportunities.
      
      - Vox also [covered](https://www.vox.com/future-perfect/469038/open-philanthropy-alexander-berger-coeffective-giving-effective-altruism) our evolution from a single-anchor funder to a resource for other philanthropists ([PDF version](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1xMXQbw_5jDh6T07kqsYBMg2pBrLcSONv/view?usp=sharing)).  

### **Additional resources**

  - [Our Progress in 2024 and Plans for 2025](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/our-progress-in-2024-and-plans-for-2025/) is a report summarizing our progress, recent challenges, achievements, strategic shifts, and updated priorities for 2025. 
  - We manage [multiple funds](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/), each focused on a different strategy for improving the world. Click into each to explore featured grants. 
  - [This article](https://medium.com/@moskov/works-in-progress-the-long-journey-to-doing-good-better-9dfb68e50868), written by Dustin Moskovitz (Coefficient’s core funder alongside Cari Tuna), captures his personal relationship to effective altruism (EA).
  - Ezra Klein’s 2021 [interview](https://drive.google.com/file/d/14I31z0KWTqCUQ5asLvqb4lM2h7QTKhO3/view) with Holden Karnofsky, one of our founders, provides a good overview of Coefficient Giving from that time. ([audio](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5QAIud17F6oQ5FCmKbrve3)) 

  

## Problems Coefficient Giving doesn’t address directly

There are many significant problems that Coefficient does not work on directly, such as climate change and racial injustice. This does not mean we think those issues are unimportant — far from it. But when deciding what causes to adopt, we don’t focus solely on the magnitude of a problem; we also consider what’s already being done and where our resources can have the greatest [marginal impact](https://probablygood.org/core-concepts/marginal-impact/).

## Key Changes in Grantmaking

The rebrand reflects the organization's evolution from working primarily with one philanthropic partner to supporting multiple major donors pursuing cost-effective, high-impact giving. The big change is that Coefficient Giving has made it easier for other donors to grow their giving at scale.

## Overview

As an administrator, you can create classification labels to apply to files stored in Drive and Gmail messages written by your users. Classification labels are metadata that can help your organization organize, find, and apply policies to files in Drive and Gmail messages.

## Supported Editions

This feature is supported in: Frontline Starter, Frontline Standard, and Frontline Plus; Business Standard and Business Plus; Enterprise Standard and Enterprise Plus; Education Standard and Education Plus; Essentials, Enterprise Essentials, and Enterprise Essentials Plus; G Suite Business.

## Types of Labels

Drive labels can be simple, like a tag. Or, they can have many structured metadata fields such as selection fields, dates, numbers, or people.

The system supports two main label types:
- **Badged Labels**: Each company can have one "badged label," which will be prominently visible as a colored rectangle in Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, providing a visual reminder to users to handle these files with care.
- **Standard Labels**: Standard labels may still represent important information and can be used to enforce policy but will not have the same visual prominence.

## Label Setup and Configuration

You can add up to 10 fields to labels to allow more granular classification. For example, a Department label could have a field with a list of options such as Finance, Engineering, and Legal.

For labels with a badged field, you can add a link to documentation about the label. Users see this "learn more" link when they point to the badged label or open the Labels pane for a file.

## Label Limits and Application

You can create up to 150 labels for your organization.

Files can have up to 5 user-applied labels. You can apply up to 20 labels total between user-applied and rule-applied labels.

## Automatic Classification Methods

There are 3 ways to automatically apply labels to files: default classification, DLP, and AI classification.

Administrators can use data loss prevention (DLP) rules to automatically apply labels to Drive files based on detection of sensitive content. Classification labels can be applied as an automatically applied DLP action, and when the DLP rule is triggered, DLP applies labels as an action to Drive files that meet the rule criteria.

Admins can configure sharing restrictions to be applied to all files with a given label through labels-driven sharing restrictions with Workspace data loss prevention (DLP) integration. Labels can help admins prevent external sharing, downloading, and printing of classified files via an integration with data loss prevention (DLP).

## How It Works

DLP rules can scan the content of files for specific patterns and automatically apply the appropriate label. For example, you can create a DLP rule that detects patterns like credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, or custom keywords specific to your business, and when a match is found, the rule automatically applies a label like "Highly Confidential".

## Important Considerations

Google automatically locks labels that are used in active DLP or retention rules. Additionally, labels applied by DLP rules take priority over those set by default classification policies.

## Key Findings: Google Drive Classification Labels — DLP, Sharing Controls, Label Locking, and Retention

---

### 1. DLP Auto-Applying Classification Labels to Drive Files

- **How it works:** DLP rules can automatically apply classification labels to Drive files as a rule *action* when sensitive content is detected. The rule scans file content and, when conditions match, stamps the file with a chosen label and a single-select Options list field value.
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/apply-classification-labels-to-drive-files-automatically-with-dlp-rules` (formerly support.google.com/a/answer/9843931, redirects as of June 2026)
- **Supported content detectors for conditions:**
  - Predefined data types: SSNs, driver's licenses, taxpayer IDs, credit card numbers (exact list varies by region; SSN and credit cards are confirmed).
  - Custom word list detectors: comma-separated terms; capitalization/symbols ignored; complete words only; 2+ letter/digit minimum.
  - Custom regex detectors: pattern-based; testable via "Test Expression" in the Admin Console.
  - Likelihood thresholds: Very high / High / Medium.
  - Minimum unique match count and total match count configurable.
  - Multiple conditions can be combined with AND/OR/NOT.
  - Metadata (file names, suggestions, existing labels) is *always* scanned.
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-dlp-for-drive-rules-and-custom-content-detectors` (formerly support.google.com/a/answer/9655387)
- **Limitations on label actions:**
  - Only Options list fields with *single selection* (multi-select disabled) are supported.
  - Cannot apply a label without also setting a field value via DLP (use default classification instead for that use case).
  - Number, Date, Text, and Person field types are not supported in DLP conditions or actions.
  - Source: both knowledge.workspace.google.com articles above.
- **Confidence: HIGH** — from primary official documentation, multiple corroborating fetches.

---

### 2. Label-Driven Sharing Restrictions via DLP

The documentation describes two distinct but related mechanisms:

**A. DLP rule actions that restrict sharing (content-triggered):**
- **Block external sharing:** Prevents the file from being shared with users outside the organization when DLP conditions match.
- **Disable download, print, and copy:** Applies to "commenters and viewers only" (editors are not restricted by this action).
- **Apply classification label:** Stamps the file with a label and field value.
- These are all selectable *actions* within a single DLP rule. The documentation does not explicitly state they can be combined in one rule, but they are listed as co-equal action options in the Admin Console rule builder (Security > Access and data control > Data protection > Manage Rules).
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-dlp-for-drive-rules-and-custom-content-detectors`

**B. Indirect label-driven sharing restriction:**
- When a DLP rule that *blocks external sharing* is active in the organization, external users (outside the org) cannot view version history of **any file that has ever had any DLP rule applied** — including DLP rules that only apply labels and do not themselves block sharing. This is a notable side effect.
  - Exact quote: *"If you have a DLP rule that blocks external sharing, users outside of your organization can't view the version history of files that have ever had any DLP rule applied to them, including DLP rules that apply labels but do not block external sharing."*
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/dlp-for-drive-faq` (formerly support.google.com/a/answer/9656855)

**C. What the documentation does NOT confirm:**
- There is no evidence in the fetched documentation of a label-level sharing restriction that operates *independently* of DLP rules (i.e., a label field that, when set, automatically enforces sharing restrictions without a DLP rule being triggered). This may exist in Trust Rules or Context-Aware Access, but was not confirmed in the sources retrieved.
- **Confidence: HIGH** for A and B. **LOW** for whether labels alone (without a DLP rule) can independently block sharing.

---

### 3. Setup Workflow: DLP Rule That Applies a Label

Based on `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-dlp-for-drive-rules-and-custom-content-detectors`:

1. **Navigate:** Admin Console > Menu > Security > Access and data control > Data protection.
2. **(Optional) Create custom detectors:** Manage Detectors > Add detector > choose Regular expression or Word list > name and save.
3. **Create rule:** Manage Rules > Add rule > New rule (or from template).
4. **Name and describe** the rule.
5. **Select apps:** Google Drive > Drive files > Continue.
6. **Configure scope:** Apply to all users, or narrow by OU/group > Continue.
7. **Add content conditions:** Add Condition > select content type ("All content"), detection method (predefined data type, word list, regex), data type, likelihood threshold, match count > Continue.
8. **Select actions:** Choose one or more of:
   - Block external sharing
   - Disable download, print, and copy (commenters and viewers)
   - Apply classification label (select the label and single-select Options list value; optionally set whether users can override/change the label value)
9. **Configure alerting:** Severity (Low/Medium/High), Alert center, email recipients (up to 50 alerts per rule per day).
10. **Set rule status:** Active or Inactive.
11. **Create.** Changes propagate within 24 hours (typically faster).

**User override option:** When configuring the Apply Label action, you can select whether users are *allowed* to change the label and field values applied by DLP ("Allow" option). If allowed and users change the label, those user-modified values persist even if the DLP rule is later disabled; only the DLP-applied values are removed.

---

### 4. Label Locking

- **What it is:** When a label, field, or field option is associated with an *active* DLP rule, Vault retention rule, default classification rule, or AI classification rule, it becomes **locked in the Label Manager.**
  - Exact quote: *"Labels, fields, and field options that are associated with DLP rules are locked in the label manager. This prevents edits to labels or fields that could break business policies."*
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/apply-classification-labels-to-drive-files-automatically-with-dlp-rules`
- **What locking blocks:**
  - Cannot disable the label.
  - Cannot delete the label, locked fields, or locked field options.
- **What locking allows:**
  - Renaming labels or fields.
  - Adding new fields or new options to an existing Options list.
- **How to unlock:** Remove the label from all DLP rules (and all other rule types that caused the lock). The lock releases automatically once no active rule references it.
- **Locking is broader than DLP alone:** The label creation docs confirm locking also triggers when labels are used in *default classification, AI classification, or Vault retention rules* — not just DLP.
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization`
- **Confidence: HIGH** — explicit quotes from primary docs.

---

### 5. Priority/Precedence: DLP > AI Classification > Default Classification

- **Exact quoted text:** *"Label values set by DLP rules take priority over AI classification, and both take priority over default classification."*
  - Source: `https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/apply-classification-labels-to-drive-files-automatically-with-dlp-rules`
- **Tie-breaking when multiple DLP rules conflict:** *"The value that's higher in the label's options list is applied."* (i.e., the order of options in the label's Options list, not rule priority number, determines which value wins in a multi-rule conflict).
- **Confidence: HIGH** — directly quoted from official source.

---

### 6. Google Vault / Retention Integration

- **Label-driven retention is supported**, introduced June 2023.

### 1. Key Findings with Sources

---

#### TAXONOMY DESIGN: How Many Tiers and Why Small Wins

- **3–5 tiers is the universal consensus.** Microsoft's formal guidance states frameworks "typically contain anywhere from three to five data classification levels" and recommends "no more than five top-level parent labels, each with five sub-labels (25 total) to keep the UI manageable." The canonical example: Public / Internal (or General) / Confidential / Highly Confidential.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-data-classification-and-labels (updated Jan 2026; confidence: **HIGH**)
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework (updated Jan 2026; confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Fewer tiers drive adoption.** Microsoft's internal pilot found users confused by a "Personal" label (was it about PII or personal matters?). They switched to "Non-business." Lesson: taxonomy doesn't need to be perfect on day 1 — pilot and adjust. Their deployment guidance explicitly says "as a best practice to lower admin overhead and reduce complexity for your users, try to keep the number of labels to a minimum."
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/get-started-with-sensitivity-labels (updated April 2026; confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Another Microsoft internal lesson:** They originally used "Internal" but found legitimate reasons documents needed external sharing, and shifted to "General." This illustrates how taxonomy names carry behavioral implications.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-data-classification-and-labels (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Varonis** recommends three functional levels (high/medium/low sensitivity) with an emphasis on simplicity, citing that "overly complex schemes create confusion and dilute adoption."
  - Source: https://www.varonis.com/blog/data-classification (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **NIST SP 800-60** (federal/government context) uses three impact levels — Low, Moderate, High — mapped across Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability using the "High Watermark Principle." This is prescriptive for federal systems but commonly referenced as a framework baseline for commercial orgs in regulated sectors.
  - Source: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/60/r2/iwd (draft Rev. 2, 2024; confidence: **HIGH** for government; **MEDIUM** for direct commercial applicability)

- **Google Workspace** uses a four-tier default (Public / Internal / Confidential / Highly Confidential) with up to 150 labels maximum per organization and up to 5 user-applied labels per file.
  - Source: https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin (confidence: **HIGH** for Google Workspace specifics)

---

#### PHASED ROLLOUT APPROACH

The consensus across Microsoft, Gravity Union, Applied Information Sciences (AIS), and Info-Tech Research Group is a "crawl-walk-run" or staged model:

**Phase 0 — Planning/Discovery (weeks 1–4):**
- Form a cross-functional virtual team (Legal, Compliance, Security, IT, Communications)
- Inventory data stores; conduct stakeholder interviews
- Define taxonomy and controls per tier
- Align with regulatory obligations (HIPAA, GDPR, PCI-DSS, etc.)
- Get executive sponsor sign-off
- Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/get-started-with-sensitivity-labels; https://www.infotech.com/research/ss/discover-and-classify-your-data

**Phase 1 — Pilot (weeks 1–4 / months 1–3):**
- Deploy labels to a small representative group (10–50 users; typically IT, Compliance, Legal, and one business unit)
- Manual labeling only; no enforcement
- Collect feedback via audit logs, help desk tickets, and user interviews
- Iterate on label names, tooltips, and protection settings
- Sources: https://www.ais.com/implementing-sensitivity-labels-in-a-highly-regulated-environment/; https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips

**Phase 2 — Expanded Rollout + Auto-Labeling (months 3–6 / weeks 5–10):**
- Roll out to broader departments with wave-based expansion
- Enable auto-labeling/DLP for well-understood sensitive data types (PII, PCI, PHI patterns)
- Set default labels for document libraries / shared drives
- Expand training to all users
- Sources: https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips; https://www.epcgroup.net/blog/microsoft-purview-information-protection-guide

**Phase 3 — Full Adoption + Enforcement (months 6–12+ / weeks 11–16+):**
- Mandatory labeling enforcement (block save/send without a label)
- Advanced automation: trainable AI classifiers, endpoint DLP, UEBA integration
- Compliance validation, audit readiness
- Governance hand-off to ongoing program
- Sources: https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips; https://www.epcgroup.net/blog/microsoft-purview-information-protection-guide

**Phase 4 — Monitor/Optimize (ongoing):**
- Regular taxonomy reviews (at minimum annually)
- KPI tracking; adjust policies for new data types and regulatory changes
- Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework

---

#### TIMELINE ESTIMATES

- **Microsoft Purview / enterprise M365:** 12–20 weeks for core deployment; add 4–6 weeks for HIPAA/FedRAMP environments.
  - Source: https://www.epcgroup.net/blog/microsoft-purview-information-protection-guide (confidence: **MEDIUM** — this is a consultancy's estimate, not Microsoft's official SLA)
  
- **Mid-market firms with automated tooling:** "weeks" for basic discovery + policy enforcement via single-agent SaaS deployment.
  - Source: https://www.sentinelone.com/cybersecurity-101/data-and-ai/what-is-data-classification/ (confidence: **MEDIUM** — vendor context)

- **General enterprise range:** 3–12 months for a comprehensive program, depending on data volume, repository diversity, regulatory complexity, and change management maturity.
  - Source: Multiple converging sources; confidence: **HIGH**

- **Info-Tech guided implementation:** 4–6 months with 5-day workshop model.
  - Source: https://www.infotech.com/research/ss/discover-and-classify-your-data (confidence: **MEDIUM**)

---

#### PILOT GROUPS

- **Why pilot first:** A narrow pilot (10–50 users across IT, Compliance, Legal, and one representative business unit) catches taxonomy problems before org-wide deployment creates confusion or over-classification at scale. AIS's documented approach uses exactly 10 users across Legal, Security, Compliance, and Engineering.
  - Source: https://www.ais.com/implementing-sensitivity-labels-in-a-highly-regulated-environment/ (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Selection criteria:** Pilot should include both "friendly" power users and skeptical/representative general users. Label policies in Microsoft Purview can be scoped to specific users/groups, making pilot rollout technically easy.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/get-started-with-sensitivity-labels (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Success gate before expansion:** Collect audit log data, gather qualitative feedback via Teams channels, measure DLP false positives, and confirm that label names/tooltips are self-explanatory before broad rollout.
  - Source: https://www.ais.com/implementing-sensitivity-labels-in-a-highly-regulated-environment/ (confidence: **HIGH**)

---

#### CHANGE MANAGEMENT AND USER ADOPTION

- **Microsoft's own data:** "Approximately 50% of an Information Protection project is business focused rather than technical." This is the single most important planning implication — under-investing in change management is the primary failure mode.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-data-classification-and-labels (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Executive sponsorship is non-negotiable.** "Having a senior stakeholder is critical for success, as many projects struggle to start or take longer without senior management backing." C-suite championing signals that classification is a shared business responsibility, not an IT edict.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework (confidence: **HIGH**)
  - Corroborated: https://avasant.com/report/overcoming-obstacles-to-data-classification/ (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Minimize user burden.** "If users need to follow complex, rigid, and time-consuming procedures ... there's always a risk that they might stop following procedures." This applies at all levels, including C-suite. Automation should do the heavy lifting; humans should manage exceptions, not do routine classification.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Training approach:** Incorporate classification into existing annual security awareness training rather than creating a standalone course. Develop super-users/champions for departments requiring manual tagging. Provide in-app tooltips and a custom "learn more" link in label policy.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **User fatigue and resistance:** When employees perceive classification as extra work interrupting workflow, resistance emerges. The ADKAR model (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement) is explicitly recommended as a change management framework for classification rollouts.
  - Source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/security-insider/emerging-trends/ai-security-guide-data-governance-and-security (confidence: **MEDIUM** — referenced in search synthesis, not independently verified in full article)

- **Communications:** Role-specific messaging is more effective than generic announcements — frame for legal teams as "compliance risk reduction," for analysts as "faster data discovery," for business units as "avoiding a breach headline."
  - Source: https://www.firstsanfranciscopartners.com/blog/change-managements-vital-role-in-a-data-management-initiative/ (confidence: **MEDIUM**)

---

#### MANUAL vs. AUTOMATED CLASSIFICATION TRADEOFFS

- **Manual labeling alone does not scale.** "Manual labeling leads to inconsistency — or worse, apathy." Users pick the easiest label, skip classification entirely, or apply the wrong tier. Manual is appropriate for high-stakes documents (legal privilege, M&A) and as a user-override mechanism.
  - Sources: Multiple (Varonis, SentinelOne, cyraacs.blogspot.com/2025); confidence: **HIGH**

- **The practical hybrid model:**
  1. **Defaults** — Apply a baseline label (e.g., "Internal") to all new files automatically. This ensures nothing is unlabeled without adding user friction.
  2. **DLP for the obvious** — Auto-classify clearly identifiable regulated data types (SSNs, credit card patterns, PHI) using pattern matching / DLP rules. Near-zero false positives for well-defined patterns.
  3. **AI/trainable classifiers for the ambiguous** — LLMs/trainable classifiers for unstructured content where pattern matching fails (contracts, IP documents, board materials). Higher false-positive rate; requires tuning.
  4. **Manual override** — Users can raise or adjust labels; policies can prevent downgrading without justification.
  - Sources: https://www.varonis.com/blog/data-classification; https://material.security/workspace-resources/google-drive-data-classification-strategies-to-protect-your-files; https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Auto-labeling limits in Purview:** Max 100 auto-labeling policies per tenant, 100,000 files labeled per day automatically. Existing files only label when opened; new files label on creation. This is a meaningful constraint for organizations with large legacy data stores.
  - Source: https://www.welkasworld.com/post/25-mistakes-you-may-be-making-with-your-sensitivity-labels (confidence: **HIGH** for Purview specifics)

- **Google Workspace AI classification (Gemini):** As of late 2025, in closed beta. Requires Enterprise Plus. Admin-defined prompts drive labeling; users can review and accept/modify. No manual training files needed (unlike older AI classification which required hundreds of samples).
  - Source: https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/gemini-data-classification-google-drive.html (confidence: **HIGH** for GWS specifics)

- **Accuracy benchmarks:** Classification accuracy target is 90–95% acceptable, 95%+ ideal. A financial services case study improved from 75% to 92% accuracy in six months via audits + training + ML integration.
  - Source: https://kpidepot.com/kpi/data-classification-accuracy (confidence: **MEDIUM** — limited sourcing on benchmarks)

- **Varonis AI accuracy claim:** Combining AI classifiers with existing deterministic rules raised their default accuracy from ~95% to ~99%.
  - Source: https://www.varonis.com/blog/whats-new-in-varonis-august-2024 (confidence: **MEDIUM** — vendor self-reported)

---

#### GOVERNANCE OWNERSHIP

- **Who owns the taxonomy and policy is a recurring governance failure point.** The standard model from Info-Tech, Netwrix, and data governance practitioners:
  - **Data Owner** (business leader / VP / Director): Accountable for the classification decision and approves exceptions. The signal of a real owner: they have signed off on at least one access denial in the past 6 months.
  - **Data Steward** (business practitioner): Responsible for day-to-day quality, develops draft taxonomy, maintains the classification standard, ensures policy is followed. This is often a Compliance or Information Governance professional.
  - **Data Custodian** (IT/Security): Implements technical controls — encryption, access provisioning, DLP, retention — aligned to classification level.
  - Sources: https://thedatagovernor.com/data-steward-vs-data-owner-vs-data-custodian/; https://netwrix.com/en/resources/guides/information-governance-data-discovery-classification/ (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **Cross-functional steering body.** Microsoft explicitly recommends involving Legal, Compliance/Privacy (including Chief Privacy Officer and Office of General Counsel), IT, Communications, and Records Management in taxonomy development. A Data Classification Steering Committee (DCSC) is the recommended governance body.
  - Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework (confidence: **HIGH**)

- **IT alone cannot own classification.** The SANS white paper abstract specifically warns against letting "information technology support organizations" unilaterally identify protection needs, because it "results in inefficient and ineffective technology-focused information protection plans that do not specifically address a company's business need."
  - Source: https://www.sans.org/white-papers/846 (2003 — older, but the principle is consistent with all current guidance; confidence: **MEDIUM** for age)

- **Annual review minimum.** Taxonomy and policies should be reviewed at minimum annually or upon major organizational/regulatory changes.
  - Source: https://www.netwrix.com/data_classification_policy_template.html; multiple corroborating sources (confidence: **HIGH**)

---

#### COMMON PITFALLS AND FAILURE MODES

Consolidated from Microsoft, Varonis, Netwrix, Fortra, cyraacs, AIS, and others:

1. **Too many tiers / label sprawl.** "More than 25 total labels typically creates user confusion and reduces adoption." If the taxonomy requires a flowchart to navigate, it will fail. Confidence: **HIGH**
2. **Over-classification / classifying everything as Confidential.** Users default to the highest label to avoid blame; this collapses the taxonomy's utility and floods DLP systems with false positives. Confidence: **HIGH**
3. **Treating it as a one-time project.** All sources emphasize classification is a continuous program. Regulations change, data landscapes evolve, user behavior shifts. Confidence: **HIGH**
4. **No executive buy-in.** Programs without a named executive sponsor lose political oxygen quickly. Confidence: **HIGH**
5. **Launching org-wide immediately without piloting.** Deploying 15+ labels to all users on day 1 causes adoption failure. Phased rollout is explicitly recommended by Microsoft, AIS, and Gravity Union. Confidence: **HIGH**
6. **Technology without training.** Automation reduces burden but does not eliminate user responsibility. Without training, even a well-designed taxonomy fails in edge cases. Confidence: **HIGH**
7. **Premature encryption.** Applying encryption to everything at Confidential level or above breaks workflows, causes productivity complaints, and drives workarounds. Apply encryption selectively (start with Highly Confidential / Restricted). Confidence: **HIGH**
8. **Focusing only on structured data.** Email, PDFs, and chat logs contain the most sensitive data but are frequently overlooked in scope. Confidence: **HIGH**
9. **Relying solely on manual labeling.** Doesn't scale. Leads to inconsistency, label skipping, and apathy. Confidence: **HIGH**
10. **Vague category definitions.** "Confidential" and "Restricted" as adjacent tiers leave users guessing. Use "Confidential" and "Highly Confidential" so the hierarchy is self-evident. Confidence: **HIGH**
11. **Authority gaps / no political clout.** Security teams often lack the organizational authority to mandate classification across all business units. Governance escalation path and executive charter are essential. Confidence: **HIGH**

Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework; https://www.varonis.com/blog/data-classification; https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips; https://cyraacs.blogspot.com/2025/05/how-to-avoid-common-pitfalls-in-data-classification.html; https://avasant.com/report/overcoming-obstacles-to-data-classification/

---

#### METRICS FOR SUCCESS

- **% of files/assets labeled (coverage):** Target full coverage over time; prioritize high-risk repositories first. Track via Purview's Activity Explorer / Data Explorer, or Google Workspace audit logs.
- **Classification accuracy rate:** % of labeled items correctly classified. Target: 90–95% minimum, 95%+ optimal.
  - Formula: (Correctly Classified Entities / Total Classified Entities) × 100
- **User adoption rate:** % of users actively applying labels; track manually applied vs. auto-applied ratio.
- **DLP policy hit rate and false positive rate:** High false positives indicate over-broad rules or label misuse; track and tune.
- **Reduction in security incidents / data exposure events** (lagging indicator; baseline before launch).
- **Helpdesk ticket volume related to classification/labeling** (leading indicator of confusion or friction — should decrease post-training).
- **Compliance audit outcomes:** Reduced findings / faster evidence collection.
- **Label distribution skew:** If >50% of labeled assets are "Highly Confidential," over-classification is likely.
- **Time to classify new data stores** (operational efficiency metric).

Sources: https://www.infotech.com/research/ss/discover-and-classify-your-data; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework; https://kpidepot.com/kpi/data-classification-accuracy; https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips (confidence: **HIGH** for metric types; **MEDIUM** for specific benchmarks)

---

#### GOOGLE WORKSPACE vs. MICROSOFT PURVIEW: PLATFORM-SPECIFIC NOTES

**Where guidance above is generic:**
- Taxonomy design (3–5 tiers), governance ownership model (owner/steward/custodian), change management principles, pilot approach, and phased rollout model apply equally to both platforms.

**Microsoft Purview-specific:**
- Auto-labeling hard limit: 100K files/day per tenant; 100 policies per tenant.
- Container labels (Teams, SharePoint sites) do not automatically propagate to document libraries — requires separate E5 configuration.
- Client-side auto-labeling (during editing) vs. service-side (at rest in SharePoint/OneDrive/Exchange) are distinct policies.
- Label priority ordering controls which label wins in conflicts.
- Source: https://www.welkasworld.com/post/25-mistakes-you-may-be-making-with-your-sensitivity-labels

**Google Workspace-specific:**
- Classification labels for Gmail reached GA in April 2025; Drive labels more mature.
- Gemini AI classification (Drive) was in closed beta as of November 2025; requires Enterprise Plus.
- DLP-applied labels override default labels (priority order matters).
- Max 150 labels per org; max 5 user-applied labels per file.
- Google's native tooling does not address ongoing access governance (who has access) — requires third-party tooling (e.g., Material Security, Nightfall) for full coverage.
- Sources: https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/04/data-classification-labels-for-gmail-generally-available.html; https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/gemini-data-classification-google-drive.html; https://material.security/workspace-resources/google-drive-data-classification-strategies-to-protect-your-files

---

### 2. Confidence Assessment

| Finding | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3–5 tiers recommended | HIGH | Direct from Microsoft, NIST, Varonis, Netwrix |
| Phased crawl-walk-run approach | HIGH | Multiple converging authoritative sources |
| 50% of IP project is business/change management | HIGH | Direct Microsoft quote from assurance docs |
| 12–20 week enterprise timeline | MEDIUM | From EPC Group consultancy, not official MS docs |
| 3–12 months general range | HIGH | Multiple converging sources |
| ADKAR framework for change management | MEDIUM | Referenced in search synthesis; not verified in primary source |
| AI accuracy 95–99% with blended approach | MEDIUM | Varonis vendor-reported; no independent studies found |
| Pilot size 10–50 users | HIGH | AIS documented; corroborated by MS guidance |
| Annual taxonomy review minimum | HIGH | Multiple sources |
| Google Workspace AI classification (Gemini) in beta | HIGH | Direct from Google Workspace Updates blog |

---

### 3. Gaps

- **No peer-reviewed or academic studies found** on manual vs. automated label accuracy in production enterprise environments. The accuracy benchmarks (90–95%) appear to be industry practitioner consensus, not rigorously measured baselines.
- **No Gartner or Forrester primary research** was accessible (paywalled). The Gartner RACI toolkit was found but not retrievable.
- **Helpdesk ticket reduction as a metric** is referenced anecdotally in practitioner literature but no published case study data found with specific pre/post numbers.
- **Google Workspace deployment guide** is sparse on phased rollout and change management methodology compared to Microsoft's extensive documentation. Google's tooling maturity for classification is roughly 2–3 years behind Purview.
- **No authoritative source found** that addresses "classification at the AI/Copilot prompt layer" — this is an emerging area (Purview + Copilot for M365 integration is mentioned but not deeply documented in accessible sources as of June 2026).

---

### 4. Surprising or Contradictory Findings

- **Microsoft's own internal "Personal" label confusion** is a notable admission in their public documentation — the taxonomy they originally deployed internally failed user testing and had to be renamed. This is unusually candid for vendor documentation and validates the "pilot first, iterate" principle strongly.

- **The 50% business / 50% technical split** (from Microsoft's assurance docs) is frequently cited but contradicts how most IT teams resource classification projects — nearly all budget goes to tooling, very little to change management. This is a systematic organizational failure mode, not just individual project failure.

- **Varonis's claim of <no pre-configuration, no ongoing policy maintenance, no manual tuning>** for their automated platform contradicts Microsoft's explicit guidance that human oversight, governance structures, and regular reviews are required even with full automation. This appears to be marketing language vs. operational reality.

- **Google Workspace's Gemini AI classification** as of November 2025 is still in closed beta for production use, meaning organizations deploying Google Workspace today should not plan on AI-automated classification being generally available — this is a significant gap vs. Microsoft Purview's more mature auto-labeling.

- **NIST SP 800-60** is specifically designed for federal information systems and maps to FISMA. Its three-tier (Low/Moderate/High) impact model is frequently cited in commercial classification frameworks, but applying it directly to commercial enterprise taxonomy is an oversimplification — the NIST model is about security categorization of systems, not a sensitivity-labeling scheme for individual documents.

---

### 5. Suggested Follow-Up Queries

1. **"Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels adoption dashboard metrics 'activity explorer' KPI tracking" — ** to find specific in-product reporting capabilities for measuring adoption.
2. **"Google Workspace classification labels vs Microsoft Purview comparison feature parity 2025 2026"** — to get a structured feature comparison for organizations choosing between platforms.
3. **"data classification 'mandatory labeling' enforcement timing enforcement gate user experience"** — to find guidance on when/how to flip from optional to mandatory labeling without causing a rebellion.
4. **"data classification program ROI cost justification budget security investment"** — to find quantified ROI models for securing executive budget.
5. **"sensitivity label 'trainable classifiers' accuracy false positive rate tuning enterprise"** — to find evidence-based guidance on AI classifier tuning and acceptable false-positive thresholds before production deployment.
6. **NIST AI RMF + data classification for AI training data governance** — emerging intersection worth researching separately if AI/ML data governance is in scope.

# Part 1 — Google Workspace / Drive classification labels (the mechanics)

## What they are
Classification labels are **metadata applied to Drive files and Gmail messages** to help organize, find, and apply policy to content. They can be a simple tag or carry structured fields. **[H]** ([Google: get started as a labels admin](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin)). Managed in the **Label Manager** (Admin console → Security → Access and data control → Label manager, or drive.google.com/labels). **[H]** ([Workspace Updates 2024-07](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/07/enable-classification-labels-on-workspace-apps.html))

## Badged vs. standard labels (CORRECTED — important)
- A **badge list field** is a field type ("pick one from a list of badges") that renders the selected value as a **colored rectangle** in Docs/Sheets/Slides/Drive — a visible handling reminder. Only **one badge list field per label**. **[H]** ([Google: create classification labels](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization))
- **The old "one badged label per organization" rule has been relaxed.** Google's 2021 launch post said one per company ([Workspace Updates 2021-12](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2021/12/enhanced-content-classification.html)), but current docs say up to **150 labels per org, "including multiple badged labels."** The constraint is now one badge *field* per label, not one badged label per org. **[H, but the change was never explicitly announced — verify in your console if it matters]**
- As of a **Nov 2025** update, badge values display in Drive list/grid views (highest-ranked badged label shows; a count icon flags additional labels). **[H]** ([Workspace Updates 2025-11](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/data-classification-labels-visible-google-drive.html))
- Admins can attach a **"learn more" documentation link** to a badge field; users see it on hover or in the Labels pane. **[H]** (create-labels page above)

## Editions (who can do what)
- **Create + manually apply labels**: Frontline Starter/Standard/Plus, Business Standard/Plus, all Enterprise editions, Education Standard/Plus, Essentials tiers. **Excluded**: Business Starter, Education Fundamentals (for manual apply). **[H]** (get-started page)
- **DLP-driven auto-labeling**: requires Frontline Standard/Plus, **Enterprise Standard/Plus**, Education Fundamentals/Standard/Plus, Enterprise Essentials Plus (+ Cloud Identity Premium). **Business Standard/Plus can create and manually apply labels but CANNOT auto-apply them via DLP.** **[H]** ([Google: DLP for Drive rules](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-dlp-for-drive-rules-and-custom-content-detectors))
- **AI classification**: see Part 2.

## Limits (verbatim from Google docs) **[H]**
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Labels per org | 150 (incl. badged) |
| Fields per label | 10 |
| Options per field | 200 |
| Labels a *user* can apply to one file | 5 |
| Total labels on a file (user + rule-applied) | 20 |
| Total labels on a Gmail message | 20 |
| Text field length | 100 chars |
| AI classification models per org | 5 |
Source: [create-labels](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/create-classification-labels-for-your-organization) + [get-started](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/get-started-as-a-classification-labels-admin). **Field types are immutable after publishing.**

## The three ways labels get applied
1. **Manual** — user right-clicks a Drive file → Labels → Apply (or File → Labels in Docs). Bulk apply up to 100 files. Needs edit access + "can apply" permission. **[H]** ([apply labels in Drive](https://support.google.com/drive/answer/13495216))
2. **Default classification** — auto-applies a label to **new** files (or on ownership change) scoped to an OU/group. **Does NOT retroactively label existing files. Only supports labels with an options-list field** (not badge/text/number/date/person). **[H]** ([default classification](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/apply-default-classification-labels-to-new-files-automatically))
3. **Rule-based (DLP)** and **AI classification** — see below.

## DLP integration, sharing controls, locking, retention
- **DLP auto-labeling**: a DLP-for-Drive rule scans content (predefined detectors for SSNs/credit cards/etc., custom word lists, regex, likelihood thresholds) and, on match, applies a label + a single-select options value. DLP label actions support **single-select options list fields only**. **[H]** (DLP-for-Drive page above)
- **Label-driven sharing controls**: a DLP rule's actions can **block external sharing** and **disable download/print/copy** (for commenters/viewers; editors unaffected) alongside applying a label. **[H]**
  - ⚠ Side effect: once any sharing-blocking DLP rule is active, external users can't view version history of **any** file that ever had **any** DLP rule applied — including label-only rules. **[H]** ([DLP for Drive FAQ](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/dlp-for-drive-faq))
  - There's no confirmed mechanism for a label to restrict sharing **on its own** without a DLP rule. **[L]**
- **Label locking**: labels/fields/options used by an active DLP, Vault retention, default-classification, or AI rule are **locked** — can't be disabled or deleted (renaming and adding options still allowed). Unlock by removing from all rules. **[H]** (create-labels + DLP pages)
- **Vault retention**: retention rules can key off a label's **date field** (since Jun 2023); litigation holds override retention. **[H]** ([Vault Drive retention](https://support.google.com/vault/answer/4388708)); whether non-date field values can trigger retention is **[M]**.
- **Audit**: Drive audit logs record label/DLP events (e.g. "DLP Rule applied Label Contract"); DLP rules support **"audit only"** mode for testing; the Security Investigation Tool inspects rule triggers. **[H]**

## Priority order when methods conflict (CORRECTED — it's 5 levels, not 3)
Verbatim hierarchy, highest wins: **(1) DLP without user-overwrite → (2) manual/user-applied → (3) DLP with user-overwrite → (4) AI classification → (5) default classification.** **[H]** ([AI classification page](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/label-google-drive-files-automatically-using-ai-classification)). Plain version: DLP beats AI beats default; manual user labels beat AI. Multi-DLP-rule ties break by **options-list order** (higher option wins), not rule number. **[H]**

# Part 2 — Google's AI classification for Drive labels

## What it actually is (key nuance)
The **generally-available** "AI classification" uses **custom models trained on YOUR org's own labeled files** (not Gemini foundation-model prompting). It extracts text (incl. OCR on images) and predicts labels. **[H]** ([AI classification admin help](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/label-google-drive-files-automatically-using-ai-classification))
- ⚠ A separate **Gemini prompt-based classification** (admin writes prompts, no training files) was announced **Nov 2025 in CLOSED BETA**. ([Workspace Updates 2025-11](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/11/gemini-data-classification-google-drive.html)) Don't assume it's GA — version-dependent for a Sept 2026 plan.

## Licensing (broader than "Enterprise Plus only")
Included with **Frontline Plus** and **Enterprise Plus**, plus the **Gemini Enterprise / Gemini Education Premium** add-ons and the **AI Security add-on**. **[H]** (admin help). The **AI Security add-on** (launched Apr 2024) extends AI classification down to **Business Standard/Plus, Enterprise Standard/Essentials**, etc. — add-on pricing is **not public** (contact sales). **[M]** ([AI Security add-on](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/04/ai-security-add-on-google-workspace.html)). Enterprise Plus list price ~$35/user/mo annual; Enterprise Standard ~$27 (no native AI classification). **[M]** ([Workspace pricing](https://workspace.google.com/enterprise/))

## Label constraint
AI classification trains on **one field per label** with **2–7 options**, published. ⚠ Two Google pages disagree on whether that field can be a badge list or **options list only** — the dedicated create-labels page says options-list only; treat that as the safer assumption. **[M]**

## Training process (this drives timeline)
- Designate **labelers**; they manually apply a **training label** (must differ from the classification label) to **≥100 files per option**, each file **≥500 characters**. More than 100/option is better. **[H]**
- System checks readiness ~24h after labeling; a **training run takes 4–6 hours** (longer for big datasets). **[H]**
- Model gets a **recall score**: **<50% = not ready; 50–80% = limited; >80% = ready.** Auto-apply allowed at ≥50% but Google recommends ≥80% on all options. **[H]**
- After enabling auto-apply: **existing** files scanned within **1–2 weeks**; new/modified files on upload/edit. **Retrains every 2 weeks** (on-demand retraining added Jul 2025). Up to **5 models/org**. **[H]** ([Jul 2025 update](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2025/07/google-drive-ai-classification-updates-multi-model-support-on-demand-model-training.html))
- ⚠ If the last eligible license lapses, the **model is deleted** (existing labels persist). **[H]**

## Privacy & accuracy
- **Privacy**: models are **customer-specific, trained only on data you designate, never used for other customers or Google's public models.** **[H]** ([Roche case study](https://workspace.google.com/blog/customer-stories/roche-protects-files-ai-classification-google-drive)); general Workspace AI privacy commitments at the [Privacy Hub](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/gemini/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub). **[H]**
- **Accuracy**: Google exposes **recall** (not precision/false-positive rate). High recall at the auto-apply gate can still mean real false positives on sensitive content — a reason to keep a human-override path. **[H for the metric gap]**. The official white paper (workspace.google.com/learning/content/gws-ai-classification-whitepaper) exists but wouldn't render for the researchers — **read it yourself if you want the architecture/accuracy detail. [L on its contents]**

**Implication for the work test:** AI classification carries a licensing cost, a multi-week training dependency (≥100 files/option + a ≥80% recall gate), false-positive risk, and a single-simple-field constraint. That's why the strong answer keeps it **off the critical path to January** — manual + default + DLP first; AI classification as a Phase-2 fast-follow on the existing backlog.

# Part 3 — How data-classification rollouts are actually run (best practices)

## Taxonomy: keep it small (3–5 tiers)
Universal consensus is **3–5 tiers**; canonical set: **Public / Internal (or "General") / Confidential / Highly Confidential.** Microsoft recommends ≤5 top-level labels (≤25 incl. sublabels) to keep adoption manageable. **[H]** ([MS data classification & labels](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-data-classification-and-labels); [MS create a framework](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/compliance/assurance/assurance-create-data-classification-framework)). Varonis: "overly complex schemes create confusion and dilute adoption." **[H]** ([Varonis](https://www.varonis.com/blog/data-classification)). Use "Confidential" vs "Highly Confidential" (not adjacent "Confidential"/"Restricted") so the hierarchy is self-evident. NIST SP 800-60 uses Low/Moderate/High but is about **system categorization**, not document labeling — don't over-map it. **[H/M]** ([NIST SP 800-60r2 draft](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/60/r2/iwd))
- Real anecdote worth borrowing: Microsoft's internal pilot renamed "Personal" → "Non-business" and "Internal" → "General" after user confusion. Taxonomy names carry behavior; pilot and iterate. **[H]** ([MS get started with sensitivity labels](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/get-started-with-sensitivity-labels))

## Phased rollout (crawl-walk-run)
0. **Discovery/plan** (≈weeks 1–4): cross-functional team, data inventory, taxonomy + per-tier controls, regulatory alignment, exec sign-off.
1. **Pilot** (10–50 users across IT/Legal/Compliance + one business unit): manual labeling, **no enforcement**, gather feedback, tune names/tooltips/false-positives.
2. **Expanded rollout + auto-labeling** (months 3–6): wave by department, enable DLP/default for well-understood data, broaden training.
3. **Full adoption + enforcement** (months 6–12+): mandatory labeling, advanced automation (AI classifiers), audit/compliance validation.
4. **Monitor/optimize** (ongoing): ≥annual taxonomy review, KPI tracking.
**[H]** (MS Purview guidance; [AIS regulated-environment rollout](https://www.ais.com/implementing-sensitivity-labels-in-a-highly-regulated-environment/); [Gravity Union rollout tips](https://www.gravityunion.com/blog/purview-sensitivity-labels-rollout-tips))

## Timelines
- Enterprise M365 core deployment ~**12–20 weeks** (consultancy estimate). **[M]** ([EPC Group](https://www.epcgroup.net/blog/microsoft-purview-information-protection-guide))
- General range **3–12 months** depending on data volume, repositories, regulation, change-management maturity. **[H]**
(For the test's Sept 2026 → Jan 2027 window ≈ 4 months: realistic for pilot + phased manual/DLP rollout; **not** enough to lean on AI-model maturity.)

## Change management is the real work
- **"~50% of an Information Protection project is business-focused, not technical."** Under-investing here is the #1 failure mode. **[H]** (MS assurance docs)
- **Executive sponsorship is non-negotiable** — projects without a named senior sponsor stall. **[H]**
- **Minimize user burden** — if labeling is tedious, users stop doing it. Automate the routine; let humans handle exceptions/overrides. **[H]**
- **Training**: fold into existing security-awareness training; use departmental champions; in-app tooltips + a "learn more" link. **[H]**
- **Role-specific messaging** beats generic announcements (legal → "compliance risk"; analysts → "faster discovery"). **[M]** ([First San Francisco Partners](https://www.firstsanfranciscopartners.com/blog/change-managements-vital-role-in-a-data-management-initiative/))

## Manual vs. automated (the hybrid everyone lands on)
1. **Default** baseline label on new files (no friction, nothing unlabeled).
2. **DLP** for clearly-detectable regulated data (SSNs, PCI, PHI) — near-zero false positives.
3. **AI/trainable classifiers** for ambiguous unstructured content (contracts, IP) — higher false-positive rate, needs tuning.
4. **Manual override** for users to raise/adjust; block downgrades without justification.
**[H]** (Varonis; [Material Security on Google Drive](https://material.security/workspace-resources/google-drive-data-classification-strategies-to-protect-your-files); Gravity Union). Manual-only "leads to inconsistency, label-skipping, and apathy" and doesn't scale. **[H]**

## Governance ownership (not IT alone)
Standard split: **Data Owner** (business leader, accountable, approves exceptions) / **Data Steward** (Compliance/Info-Gov, maintains taxonomy + standard) / **Data Custodian** (IT/Security, implements controls). A **steering committee** (Legal, Privacy, Compliance, IT, Comms, Records) owns the taxonomy. SANS explicitly warns against IT unilaterally defining protection needs. **[H]** ([data owner/steward/custodian](https://thedatagovernor.com/data-steward-vs-data-owner-vs-data-custodian/); [Netwrix info-governance guide](https://netwrix.com/en/resources/guides/information-governance-data-discovery-classification/); [SANS 846](https://www.sans.org/white-papers/846))

## Common pitfalls (all **[H]** unless noted)
Label sprawl / too many tiers · over-classification (everyone picks "Highly Confidential" → DLP false-positive flood) · treating it as one-time vs. ongoing · no exec buy-in · org-wide launch with no pilot · tech without training · premature blanket encryption (breaks workflows) · ignoring email/PDF/chat · manual-only · vague tier names · no governance authority.

## Success metrics
% files/users labeled (coverage) · classification accuracy (target 90–95%+, **[M]** on benchmark) · adoption rate (manual vs auto ratio) · DLP hit & false-positive rate · incident reduction (lagging) · **helpdesk ticket volume on labeling** (leading friction signal — should fall after training) · audit outcomes · label-distribution skew (>50% "Highly Confidential" = over-classification). **[H]** for metric types, **[M]** for specific targets.

## Google Workspace vs. Microsoft Purview (context)
The generic principles (tiers, governance, change mgmt, phased pilot) apply to both. Google's classification tooling is **~2–3 years behind Purview in maturity**; Google labels don't natively cover access governance (who-has-access) — third-party tools (Material, Nightfall) fill that. Gmail labels hit GA Apr 2025; Gemini Drive classification was beta Nov 2025. **[H/M]** (Material Security; Workspace Updates)

1. **Badged labels per org**: 2021 blog "one per company" vs. current "150 incl. multiple badged." The relaxation wasn't formally announced — confirm in-console if it matters.
2. **AI classification field type**: admin-help page says "badge list OR options list"; create-labels page says "options list only." Assume options-list-only to be safe.

5. **Accuracy benchmarks (90–95%)**: practitioner consensus, not rigorous studies; Google publishes recall, not precision/false-positive rates.
6. **12–20 week timeline**: consultancy estimate, not an official SLA.
7. **Vault retention on non-date label fields**: documented for date fields; broader support unconfirmed.
